title: Immutable updates: change the data, not the copy
objectives: Explain that spread copies one level, and write nested updates that copy every level on the path to the change
Choose copying array methods (`map`, `filter`, `toSorted`, `toSpliced`, `with` — ES2023) over mutating ones (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`)
Choose between a targeted update, `structuredClone` and `Object.freeze`, knowing what `structuredClone` can't clone and that `freeze` is shallow
Predict how mutation breaks React: the `Object.is` bail-out skips the update, and StrictMode's double reducer call doubles a `push`

sources.title: MDN: Array — copying methods and mutating methods
React docs: Updating Arrays in State
React docs: Updating Objects in State

questions.prompt: `const next = { ...state, count: 2 }; next.user.name = "Grace";` — what is `state.user.name` now?

options.text: `"Grace"` — the spread copied the reference to `user`, so both point at one object
Unchanged — spread makes a deep copy
It throws, because spread freezes the copied properties
Unchanged, because only `count` was overridden in `next`

questions.explanation: Spread creates one new outer object and copies each property's value into it — and for `user` that value is a reference. `next.user` and `state.user` are the same object, so writing through either changes both. To change a nested field, copy that level too: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name: "Grace" } }`.

questions.prompt: In plain JavaScript, `setTags(tags.push("new"))`. What does the component render next?

options.text: Broken: `push` returns the new length, so `tags` becomes a number (and the old array was mutated too)
The tags plus `"new"` — `push` returns the updated array
The old tags — `push` returns `undefined`, which React ignores
The tags plus `"new"`, because `push` returns a copy

questions.explanation: `push` mutates the array in place and returns its new **length**. The state becomes a number (`tags.map` then throws), while the original array silently gained an item. TypeScript would reject the call (`number` isn't `string[]`), which is one reason to type state. The copy that says what you mean: `setTags([...tags, "new"])`.

questions.prompt: A component renders `{users.sort(byName).map(…)}`, where `users` is a prop. What's wrong?

options.text: `sort` reorders the parent's array in place, during render; use `users.toSorted(byName)` (ES2023) or `[...users].sort(byName)`
`sort` returns `undefined`, so `.map` throws
Nothing is wrong, it's only slow — wrap it in `useMemo`
`sort` without a comparator sorts by string, so it needs `localeCompare`

questions.explanation: `sort` sorts in place and returns the same array, so this mutates data the parent owns — every other reader of `users` now sees it sorted — and if `users` is the parent's state, that state changed without a `setState`. `useMemo` would cache the mutation, not prevent it. (A comparator *is* passed here, and `sort` returns the array, not `undefined`.) `toSorted` returns a sorted copy.

questions.prompt: `structuredClone(form)`, where `form` holds a `Date`, a `Map`, and an `onSave` callback. What happens?

options.text: It throws a `DataCloneError` — functions can't be cloned
It copies everything except `onSave`, which is silently dropped
It copies everything, the callback included
It copies everything, but the `Date` becomes an ISO string

questions.explanation: The structured clone algorithm can't duplicate functions (or DOM nodes); MDN says attempting it throws a `DataCloneError`, so the whole call fails. Silently dropping functions and turning dates into strings is what the old `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` trick does. `structuredClone` keeps `Date` and `Map` as real `Date` and `Map` objects.

questions.prompt: A teammate writes every reducer case as `const next = structuredClone(state); /* mutate next */ return next;`. It's correct. What does it cost?

options.text: Every object gets a new identity, changed or not, so every `memo` child, selector and effect sees a change
Nothing: React compares state by contents, so unchanged parts are detected
`structuredClone` is asynchronous, so the update lands a frame late
StrictMode's double call would clone twice and duplicate items

questions.explanation: React and its ecosystem compare by identity (`Object.is`), not contents. A targeted update keeps unchanged parts as the same objects, which is what lets them skip work; a deep clone makes everything look changed, on every action. Cloning is synchronous, and a pure function that clones is safe to call twice. Keep `structuredClone` for independent snapshots — a draft, an undo entry.

questions.prompt: In an ES module: `const config = Object.freeze({ api: { retries: 3 } }); config.api.retries = 5;` — what happens?

options.text: `retries` becomes 5 — `freeze` only froze the outer object
A `TypeError`, because modules are strict and `config` is frozen
The write is silently ignored
`retries` becomes 5 on a copy; `freeze` returned a frozen clone

questions.explanation: `Object.freeze` is shallow: `config`'s own properties are locked, but `config.api` is a separate object that was never frozen. The `TypeError` (modules are strict) would come from writing `config.api = …` or `config.x = …`; in sloppy-mode scripts that write would be silently ignored instead. And `freeze` returns the same object, not a copy. Freezing deeply needs a recursive walk.

questions.prompt: `items.push(item); setItems(items);` — the list on screen doesn't change. Why?

options.text: React compares the new state with `Object.is`; it's the same array, so React skips the re-render
State updates are asynchronous; it will appear after the next tick
React deep-compares the arrays and found them equal
`push` created a new array that was never passed to `setItems`

questions.explanation: The array was mutated, but `setItems` received the very same array, and React's `Object.is` check treats "same reference" as "no change". React never deep-compares. The update isn't merely delayed — it shows up only when something else re-renders the component. Pass a new array: `setItems([...items, item])`.

questions.prompt: A reducer does `state.todos.push(action.todo); return { ...state };`. In development every Add shows the todo twice; in production, once. Why?

options.text: StrictMode calls reducers twice in development; both calls push into the one shared array
It's a React development-build bug; production is correct
The dev server registers each click twice
`{ ...state }` copies the todos array twice

questions.explanation: React's docs: in Strict Mode, React calls your reducer twice (development only) and keeps one result, to surface impure reducers. A pure reducer returns the same answer both times. This one mutates `state.todos`, which both calls share, so the second push lands on top of the first. The duplicate is StrictMode working as intended — fix the reducer: `todos: [...state.todos, action.todo]`.

prompts.prompt: Toggle one todo without mutating: a new array, a new object for the changed todo, and the same objects for the rest.
prompts.explanation: `map` returns a new array; the callback returns a spread copy for the todo that changes and the original object for every other one, so unchanged todos keep their identity.

prompts.prompt: Get the users in name order without reordering the array you were given (ES2023).
prompts.explanation: `toSorted` returns a sorted copy. `sort` sorts in place and returns the same array, so it would reorder `users` for everyone holding it. Before ES2023: `[...users].sort(…)`.

prompts.prompt: Replace the row at `index` with `updatedRow`, returning a new array (ES2023).
prompts.explanation: `with(index, value)` is the copying version of `rows[index] = value`. It throws a `RangeError` for an index outside the array, where an assignment on a copy would silently grow it. `toSpliced(index, 1, updatedRow)` also works.

prompts.prompt: Remove the todo with this `id`, returning a new array.
prompts.explanation: `filter` keeps the items for which the callback returns `true` and builds a new array. `splice` would cut the item out of the original array in place.

prompts.prompt: Take an independent deep copy of a saved form for a draft — one that keeps `Date` and `Map` values as they are.
prompts.explanation: `structuredClone` copies every level and keeps `Date`, `Map`, `Set` and cycles, which a JSON round trip loses. It throws on functions, and class instances come back without their methods.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `count` was overridden on the new outer object, so `state.count` stays 1. But `user` was copied as a reference: `next.user` *is* `state.user`, so renaming through `next` renames the original. One level copied, the rest shared.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `sort` sorts the array in place and returns that same array, so `original` is now sorted and `sorted` is just another name for it. `original.toSorted()` (ES2023) would return a new sorted array and leave `original` as `[3, 1, 2]`. (`sort` with no comparator compares as strings — `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`.)

code: const copy = structuredClone({ at: new Date(0), price: new Money(250) });
console.log(copy.at instanceof Date, copy.price instanceof Money, typeof copy.price.format);
snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `Date` is one of the built-in types the structured clone algorithm knows, so it comes back as a real `Date`. A class instance doesn't: the prototype chain isn't copied, so `price` is a plain `{ cents: 250 }` — not a `Money`, and with no `format` method. Rebuild class instances after cloning (`new Money(copy.price.cents)`), or keep plain data in state.

code: // Rendered inside <StrictMode>, in development (React 19). The user clicks Add once.
snippets.question: What does the paragraph show?
snippets.explanation: In Strict Mode, development builds call the reducer twice with the same `state` and keep one result. Both calls push into the same `state.todos` array, so it ends up with two items, and the new outer object makes React render them. In production the reducer runs once and you'd see `milk` — which is why this bug "only happens locally". With `todos: [...state.todos, action.text]` both calls build their own array from the untouched original.
